issues.issue: "their affiliated chapter 11 debtors and debtors in possession" defines "Debtors" by reference only to a footnote list, leaving it uncertain whether non-filing Aeropostale affiliates (and Aeropostale Canada Corp., shown with no case number) are bound. The scope of "Debtors" drives every obligation in sections 1-3 and the releases in section 5.

This recital names only Aeropostale, Inc. and Aeropostale Procurement Company as parties to the Sourcing Agreement, yet the operative terms (section 1(c) payment, section 6 no-new-orders, section 8(m)) impose Sourcing Agreement duties on "the Debtors" collectively. A court could be asked whether the recital limits which Debtors are bound by the amended Sourcing Agreement.

The defined term is introduced with an unclosed quotation mark — (the "Bankruptcy Court) — a punctuation error in the very words creating the definition used throughout sections 4, 7 and 8. The defect is mechanical and unlikely to change meaning, but it is on the face of the provision.

"or earlier as described below" points to no identified provision and cannot be squared with section 1(b), which makes acceleration depend on the Debtors' written election, and with section 2, which compels the Debtors to accept early deliveries MGF attempts unilaterally. Whether MGF may deliver early of its own accord is left open by reading the two together.

The definition fixes the Detailed Delivery Schedule as the May 9, 2016 summary sheet and excel support attached as Exhibit A, while section 7 obliges the Debtors to file "a revised version of Exhibit A" with the Settlement Motion. Which version governs deliveries, prices and the discount calculations is not resolved.

"Open Commitments," "Open CPOs", "Open Orders", "US Released for Delivery" and "Orders in Transit" are given no content in the Agreement at all, only a cross-reference to categories on a spreadsheet. Because the 8% discount in section 1(c) and the early-delivery duty in section 2 turn on these categories, their boundaries are left to extrinsic material.

MGF must accelerate deliveries or change shipping method "where possible," a standard with no benchmark — commercially practicable, physically possible, or possible at MGF's convenience. The provision also leaves "sole risk of any delivery delays" undefined as to chargebacks and rejection rights.

"NDCs" is used in quotation marks as though defined but is never expanded or defined anywhere in the Agreement. The acknowledgement that NDCs "assume ocean freight" therefore has no fixed referent against which section 1(b)'s shipping-method changes can be measured.

The clause simultaneously obliges payment "at full contract price" and subjects it to "an 8.00% discount on all Open CPOs and Open Commitments, to be applied on a pro rata basis ... from the first delivery to the last delivery," without specifying how the pro rata spread is computed or against which invoices. The mechanics of the discount are the sort of thing parties litigate over invoice by invoice.

The carve-out turns on Goods being in "US Released for Delivery" or "Orders in Transit" status "on the Detailed Delivery Schedule," but never fixes the date at which status is determined — the May 9 snapshot or status at actual delivery. Goods that move between categories could be billed at full price or at the 8% discount on either reading.

"front load the production and deliveries ... to the extent practicable" sets no measurable obligation and no benchmark for practicability. Nothing in the Agreement says by how much or against what baseline licensee orders must be advanced.

The 10% licensee discount is excused for "minor ordinary course delays of less than two weeks consistent with past practice," a double standard (duration plus past practice) with no defined past practice to measure against. Whether a thirteen-day delay that is not "ordinary course" triggers the discount is unresolved on these words.

"no reductions and no cherry-picking" is an undefined colloquialism sitting against an express parenthetical preserving Sourcing Agreement adjustments for defective and non-conforming product, so the line between a permitted adjustment and prohibited cherry-picking is unfixed. The ten-day late-delivery proviso also does not say whether lateness is measured per purchase order or per shipment.

Compelling the Debtors to accept any Open Order Goods MGF attempts to deliver early cannot readily be squared with section 1(b), which makes acceleration of deliveries contingent on the Debtors' written election and at the Debtors' cost and risk. It also interacts with section 3, advancing the Debtors' fourteen-day payment clock at MGF's unilateral option.

The cash-in-advance trigger depends on an Event of Default "caused by or related to any breach by MGF" and on cure or waiver "within ten (10) calendar days," leaving unclear both the breadth of "related to" and whether the cash-in-advance regime ever ends once triggered. Whose conduct caused a DIP default, and the consequence for payment terms, is precisely the dispute these words invite.

Payment must go to the account "designated by MGF in writing on or prior to the date hereof," with no provision for the case where no such pre-closing designation was made. The words make a condition of a fact the Agreement never establishes.

The license trigger is "a liquidation of all or substantially all of the Debtors' retail stores and/or the merchandise held for sale therein," a vague threshold whose "and/or" leaves it uncertain whether a store-closing program short of a full chain wind-down qualifies. The Commencement Date also depends on an agency agreement that may never exist in the form contemplated.

The clause says the "run-off license shall provide that" MGF may complete manufacture and sell, language suggesting a separate license instrument yet to be delivered rather than the grant already made in the preceding sentence. Whether any further document is required, and who drafts it, is left open (and the text contains the error "in it sole discretion").

This condition cannot be squared with the grant in section 4's first sentence, which calls the run-off license "irrevocable" and "fully paid up"; a denial of the DIP Financing would strip a license the grant says cannot be revoked. Which sentence controls a license already commenced is unresolved.

"Sycamore Partners or any of its affiliates" leaves the antecedent of "its" ambiguous among the three named objectors, and "the Court" is used where the Agreement elsewhere defines "Bankruptcy Court." The set of objections that can defeat the license therefore has no fixed boundary.

The carve-out preserves "Claims arising out of the non-performance of any obligations set forth in this Settlement Agreement," a term never defined (the instrument defines itself as "this Agreement"), so it is unclear whether it reaches the superseded May 16 agreement or the Sourcing Agreement as amended. Against a release of all claims "known or unknown," the reach of that exception is the whole question.

The Debtors reserve defenses to Unpaid Pre-Petition Claims expressly "not based on delivery delays," which sits awkwardly with section 2 and section 8(d), which preserve the Debtors' right to reject deliveries ten or more days late as non-conforming. Whether a late-delivery defense survives as to pre-petition goods depends on reading the two together.

"THE GENERAL RELEASE" is not a defined term anywhere in the Agreement — section 5(a) and 5(b) grant two separate releases — so it is unclear which release(s) this carve-out narrows. Its reach over "ANY OF THEIR AFFILIATES (OTHER THAN MGF)" also has to be reconciled with section 5(a)'s statement that no MGF affiliate is a MGF Releasor.

Saying the general release "WILL NOT AFFECT THE AMOUNT OF THE OBLIGATIONS" under the Term Loan leaves open whether it affects anything else about those obligations — validity, priority, or enforceability. The provision also uses the undefined "GENERAL RELEASE" and contains several misspellings of the named agent and borrower.

The parties waive California Civil Code Section 1542 in an agreement that section 8(l) makes governed by New York law without regard to conflicts principles. A court could be asked what effect, if any, the waiver of an inapplicable California statute has on the scope of the releases.

"any new orders" is not defined against the existing categories of Open Orders, Open CPOs and Open Commitments, so whether revisions, reissues or replacement purchase orders for scheduled Goods count as "new" is unfixed. The boundary matters because section 8(m) keeps the Sourcing Agreement otherwise in force.

The Debtors must notify licensees that "they will not be permitted" to submit new orders, without a deadline, a form of notice, or any statement of who imposes the prohibition on these third parties. The clause also sits against section 1(d), which contemplates continuing licensee orders being front-loaded and discounted.

Automatic termination keyed to the last delivery and final payment cannot be squared with section 7, under which the entire Agreement becomes "of no further force or effect" if the Settlement Order is not entered by May 30, 2016, and with section 8(m)'s "until terminated in accordance with this Agreement." What terminates the Sourcing Agreement if deliveries are never completed is left unresolved.

The termination fee, shortfall and rebate provisions die only when the Settlement Order "becomes a final order," a term the Agreement never defines (non-appealable, or merely entered). Section 7 separately requires only entry of an approving order by May 30, leaving a gap in which those Sourcing Agreement provisions remain alive.

MGF's unconditional agreement not to assert termination fee or shortfall claims sits against the preceding sentence, which extinguishes those Sourcing Agreement provisions only when the Settlement Order becomes a final order. Whether the waiver is likewise conditioned on finality can only be answered by reading the two together.

The Debtors' rebate waiver is stated unconditionally while the preceding sentence ties the death of the rebate provisions to the Settlement Order becoming a final order. A court could be asked whether the waiver survives a failure of finality under section 7.

The duty to comply "pending approval" of the Agreement cannot easily be squared with the last sentences of section 7, under which the Agreement becomes of no force if approval is denied and only the payment obligations survive. What becomes of performance rendered in the interim, and of the releases, is left to inference.

"all actions necessary to comply with its production and delivery obligations for all of the Goods" sets an absolute standard with no force-majeure or practicability qualifier, in contrast to the "where possible" and "to the extent practicable" standards in sections 1(b) and 1(d). Which standard governs MGF's pre-approval performance is open.

The Debtors promise to "seek the Settlement Motion's approval by the Bankruptcy Court on May 23, 2016," a date entirely within the court's control rather than the promisor's, with no standard for what counts as having sought approval. The obligation to file a "revised version of Exhibit A" also leaves the content of the revision unconstrained.

The Agreement fails unless an order is entered "in form and substance reasonably acceptable to MGF," a subjective condition giving MGF latitude to declare an entered order unacceptable. Whether reasonableness is measured objectively, and who bears the burden, is not stated.

The survival proviso refers to "MGF's obligation to provide 14 day payment terms," but section 3 casts the fourteen-day term as the Debtors' payment obligation, not an MGF obligation; the words mis-assign the duty. It also ignores section 3's cash-in-advance proviso, which may already have displaced fourteen-day terms.

"its objection to the DIP Financing" does not identify which objection is withdrawn, and section 8(b) refers instead to an objection filed on behalf of Aero Investors LLC and MGF Holdings, Limited. Whether the affiliates' objection survives MGF's deemed withdrawal — which matters to the section 4 run-off license condition — is left open.

The discovery stay runs only "pending the May 23, 2016 hearing," with no provision for an adjourned or continued hearing or for the period between hearing and ruling. If the hearing moves, the duration of the stay has no stated boundary.
